pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Symbiosis (ages 9–11): close, long-term relationships between different species, classified by WHO benefits — mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other unaffected), parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense).
• Standards — UK (DfE): enriches Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (how living things depend on each other) and Y6 adaptation/interdependence; a lens on ecological relationships.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS2-2 (patterns of interactions among organisms — competitive, predatory, and mutually beneficial) is the direct anchor; builds on 3-LS4-3.
• Operational details: teach the three types via a +/0/– outcome for each partner — mutualism (+/+): clownfish–anemone, oxpecker–buffalo, bee–flower, cleaner wrasse; commensalism (+/0): remora on shark, barnacles on whale, birds nesting in trees; parasitism (+/–): ticks/fleas, tapeworms, cuckoo brood parasitism. Emphasise these are close, ongoing relationships between DIFFERENT species (not predation, which is a quick kill, and not members of the same species). Have pupils classify novel scenarios by tracking each partner's cost/benefit.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~9): define symbiosis and give one example. B (transitional, ~10): distinguish mutualism, commensalism, parasitism with an example of each. C (formal, ~11): classify a NEW relationship by determining the outcome (+/0/–) for each partner, and justify.
bestPractices: Anchor classification on a two-partner outcome grid (+ / 0 / – for each species) so pupils DECIDE the type from consequences rather than recalling labels.
Use borderline/novel cases (is a bird nesting in a tree commensalism? does the tree lose anything?) to make pupils reason rather than pattern-match to memorised pairs.
Contrast symbiosis with predation and competition so 'a lion eating a zebra' isn't miscalled symbiosis — symbiosis is a CLOSE, ongoing relationship.
Note that commensalism is often the hardest to verify (the 'unaffected' partner may be slightly affected), modelling scientific caution about clean categories.
keyRepresentations: A two-partner outcome grid: rows = species A/B, cells marked + / 0 / –, defining each symbiosis type.
Paired-organism illustrations for each type (clownfish–anemone, remora–shark, tick–deer).
A classification decision path: 'Does partner A benefit? Does partner B lose?' → type.
A relationship spectrum from mutual benefit through neutral to harm.
commonMisconceptions: 'Symbiosis always means both animals help each other' — mutualism does, but parasitism harms one partner and commensalism helps only one.
'A predator eating prey is symbiosis' — predation is a brief lethal act, not a close ongoing relationship.
'Parasites want to kill their host' — most parasites keep the host alive; a dead host is a lost home/food supply.
'Commensalism means no effect at all ever' — the second partner is not clearly benefited or harmed, but effects can be subtle/hard to measure.
'Only animals form symbioses' — many involve plants, fungi, and microbes (bee–flower, coral–algae, gut bacteria).

learn.summary: Pupils aged 9–11 learn to classify symbiosis — close, long-term relationships between different species — by reasoning from the outcome for each partner (benefit +, no clear effect 0, or harm –) rather than recalling labels. Mutualism is +/+, commensalism +/0, and parasitism +/–. The core skill is classifying a NEW pair by asking 'what does each side gain or lose?', while distinguishing symbiosis from a quick predatory kill or from competition within a species.

activities.title: Classify the relationship from outcomes
feedback: If a learner labels remora–shark as mutualism, prompt: apply the benefit test to the SECOND partner — does the shark actually gain anything? If it is unaffected, it is commensalism.

If a learner calls the tick a predator or a lion-eating-zebra parasitism, contrast the two: a predator kills and eats quickly; a parasite lives on or in a host over time, usually without killing it outright.
If a learner excludes the tick as 'not really symbiosis', restate that symbiosis is any close, long-term relationship between different species and parasitism is one of its kinds.

If a learner says the clownfish and anemone 'agree' to help each other, explain the benefit as an evolved relationship, not a conscious deal — each partner simply does what helps itself and both happen to gain.
On a borderline case, affirm that choosing 'not enough evidence' is good scientific caution: commensalism is often the hardest to verify because the 'unaffected' partner may be slightly affected.
activities.rationale: Deciding the category from consequences, and testing it on unseen pairs, builds the classification skill the standards target, and directly addresses the 'symbiosis = both help' and 'predation = symbiosis' misconceptions by forcing the benefit/harm test rather than pattern-matching memorised pairs.
sourceClaims: Patterns of interactions among organisms across ecosystems include competitive, predatory, and mutually beneficial relationships.
Symbiosis is classified as mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0), and parasitism (+/–), with canonical examples (clownfish–anemone, remora–shark, tick–host).
Most parasites do not kill their host outright, since the host is their ongoing habitat/resource; predation is distinct from symbiosis.
learnerActions: For each presented pair — clownfish and anemone, remora and shark, tick and deer, a bird nesting in a tree — mark the outcome for EACH partner as benefit (+), no clear effect (0), or harm (–).
Read off the resulting type from the two marks: +/+ = mutualism, +/0 = commensalism, +/– = parasitism.
Meet a brand-new pair (e.g. barnacles on a whale) you were not taught and classify it yourself by asking 'does the whale lose anything?'
When a card shows predation (a lion eating a zebra) or competition between members of the same species, reject it as NOT symbiosis and say why.
On deliberately fuzzy cases, choose a 'not enough evidence' response if the second partner's gain or loss is genuinely hard to tell.
activities.intendedInsight: The three vocabulary words become a reusable reasoning tool: any close, ongoing relationship between different species can be classified by tracking each partner's cost or benefit, so a harmful case (parasitism) still counts as symbiosis.

activities.title: Gallery of paired organisms (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner only reads revealed answers, prompt them to predict first, then check — reveals should confirm their reasoning, not replace it.
Highlight that a static reveal tells you the answer; the real test is classifying a pair whose outcomes you have not been given.
activities.rationale: An example gallery supports the example-driven content and seeds classification, but revealing the type hands the answer to the child; as a proposed sequence it is intended to work best as a precursor to independent classification, not a substitute.
learnerActions: Explore illustrated species pairs — clownfish–anemone, remora–shark, tick–deer, barnacle–whale — including symbioses with a non-animal partner: bee–flower, coral–algae, and gut bacteria in an animal's gut.
Reveal each partner's gain or loss — e.g. tapping a partner to show what it gains or loses — and note the resulting type.
After exploring, predict the type for the NEXT pair before revealing the outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: Concrete canonical examples build a stock of cases and show that symbioses can involve non-animal partners too — a plant (bee–flower), algae (coral–algae) and microbes (gut bacteria) — not only animals.

activities.title: Sort and classify check
feedback: For a mislabelled sort, ask the learner to state each partner's + / 0 / – before re-sorting.
For a rejected-distractor miss, restate that symbiosis is a close, ongoing relationship, unlike a brief lethal predatory act.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching can catch the 'symbiosis = both help' and 'predation = symbiosis' errors; this activity checks recognition of the distinctions rather than eliciting independent construction of a classification, so it is proposed for use after the classification activity.
learnerActions: Sort a set of pairs into mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.
Answer a multiple-choice item classifying a new scenario and justify the choice.
Reject distractor cards showing predation or same-species competition as not-symbiosis.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can distinguish the three types and holds the boundary that predation and competition are not symbiosis.

activities.title: Marine-biologist-in-role: is this really commensalism? (optional hook)
feedback: Reward learners who name a specific measurable effect that would move a case from commensalism toward mutualism or parasitism.
If a learner insists every case is clear-cut, offer a borderline case where the second partner's effect is plausibly non-zero.
activities.rationale: Dialogue about fuzzy cases can model scientific caution about categories and explore nuance; the proposed main approach manipulates outcomes directly, so this role-play is intended as a complement rather than the main activity.
learnerActions: In a short role-play discussion, argue whether a given relationship (e.g. barnacles on a whale) is truly commensalism.
Raise ways the 'unaffected' partner might actually be slightly helped or harmed, and what evidence would settle it.
activities.intendedInsight: Clean categories are a scientific simplification — commensalism is genuinely hard to verify, and good classification admits uncertainty.

constraints: The gallery and any tap-to-reveal of the type is a scaffold: because it supplies the answer, it does not on its own show whether a learner can classify independently — follow it with unseen pairs.
Sorting and multiple-choice checks test recognition of the distinctions; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of a classification from first principles.
Keep 'not enough evidence' available for genuinely borderline commensalism cases rather than forcing a clean label.
Include at least one harmful (parasitism) case among items to classify, so learners must accept a harmful relationship as symbiosis.
Keep predation and same-species competition as distractors that must be rejected, to hold the boundary of what a close, ongoing relationship is.
Include symbioses with a non-animal partner (bee–flower, coral–algae, gut bacteria) so learners do not conclude only animals form symbioses.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all four sources carry verified:false in the row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted '3D adds no conceptual value' and framed static/quiz artefacts as merely testing rather than building skill; these catalog-fit judgements are softened to scoped claims about affordances and are not established comparative-efficacy findings. The 3D illustrative pair scene is noted as an alternative but not developed as a full activity.

The gallery-as-precursor (activity 2) and sort-after-classification (activity 3) orderings are proposed instructional sequences, not source-verified findings. sourceClaims were cleared on activities 2 and 3 because the available claims support the classification content/examples, not the scaffold-sequencing or assessment-pedagogy principles those rationales rest on; the canonical-examples claim still backs the content those activities use.

Source claims about canonical examples and parasite behaviour are cited from unverified standard references; treat the +/0/– classifications of specific pairs (e.g. commensalism of barnacle–whale or remora–shark) as the textbook simplification the pedagogy itself flags as hard to verify.

probeDeeper: Which kind of symbiosis is the tick-and-deer relationship? How did you decide?
Is a lion eating a zebra symbiosis? Why or why not?
A remora rides a shark and eats its leftover scraps, but the shark isn't bothered. Which kind is that, and how is it different from clownfish-and-anemone?
Do the clownfish and anemone 'agree' to help each other? If not, how does the relationship work?
assess.correctAnswer: They are wrong. Symbiosis means any close, long-term relationship between two different species, and it comes in kinds depending on who benefits: mutualism (both gain, like clownfish and anemone), commensalism (one gains and the other is unaffected, like a remora riding a shark), and parasitism (one gains at the other's expense, like the tick harming the deer). The tick-and-deer relationship is parasitism — which is a type of symbiosis — so symbiosis is not only about helping.

errorPatterns.pattern: Symbiosis means two species helping each other, or being friends
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define symbiosis as any close relationship between species, then place mutualism, commensalism and parasitism as its three kinds.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — that isn't symbiosis, because symbiosis only means animals that help each other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Excludes parasitism; insists the tick 'doesn't count' as symbiosis.

errorPatterns.pattern: Parasitism is the same as a predator eating its prey
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two — a predator kills and eats quickly; a parasite lives on or in a host over time, usually without killing it outright.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the tick a predator, or classifies a lion eating a zebra as parasitism.

errorPatterns.pattern: In mutualism the animals decide to help each other or agree to cooperate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain the benefit as an evolved relationship, not a conscious agreement — each partner simply does what helps itself, and both happen to gain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the partners as making a deal or consciously choosing to help.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any one-sided-looking partnership is mutualism (remora and shark counted as 'both benefit')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Apply the benefit test to the SECOND partner — if it is unaffected, it's commensalism, not mutualism.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels remora-and-shark as mutualism without checking whether the shark actually gains.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks symbiosis just means animals helping each other or being friends; excludes parasitism and can't classify a new example.
responseLevels.full: Defines symbiosis as any close relationship between different species, distinguishes mutualism, commensalism and parasitism by who benefits or is harmed, correctly classifies new scenarios (including harmful ones as symbiosis), and separates parasitism from predation.
responseLevels.partial: Defines the three types and gives a memorised example of each, but stumbles on new scenarios — mislabelling remora-shark as mutualism or calling a parasite a predator — listing the categories without applying the benefit/harm test.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A tick lives on a deer, drinking its blood and giving nothing back. Some people say symbiosis only means animals helping each other, so this can't be symbiosis. Are they right? Is the tick-and-deer relationship symbiosis — and if so, what kind?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks symbiosis means mutual help denies the tick example counts, or tries to reclassify it. A child who understands says it IS symbiosis (parasitism) and classifies by the pattern of benefit and harm. Correctly admitting a harmful relationship as symbiosis is the discriminator.
